title: CFA Ethics 4: GIPS Standards - the rules for presenting investment performance
subtitle: Why an advertised "30% average annual return" is almost always worth a second look
whyItMatters: GIPS (Global Investment Performance Standards) is the CFA Institute framework that makes investment firms report performance honestly and comparably - understanding GIPS lets you spot a dressed-up performance figure the moment you read a marketing document.
openingQuestion: A fund manager advertises "an average 45% a year over the past 5 years" but quotes the result of only 1 of the 20 funds it runs (the best-performing one). What is the biggest GIPS problem here?
openingOptions: No problem at all, because the number is true: that fund genuinely earned it
It breaks the composite rule - every account on that strategy must be reported
It is only a problem if the firm has no licence to operate as a manager
GIPS applies only to publicly listed funds, so it does not reach this case at all
explanation: This is precisely what GIPS was designed to stop: "cherry-picking" the attractive number. GIPS requires a compliant firm to group every account with a similar investment strategy into a "composite" and to report the performance of that entire composite, rather than putting forward the single best-performing fund as though it represented the whole firm.

summary.keyIdea: GIPS secures the honesty and comparability of performance reporting through a rule that forces accounts into composites instead of allowing attractive numbers to be selected.
summary.commonMistake: Confusing GIPS compliance with a guarantee of good performance - GIPS only guarantees that the numbers are CALCULATED and REPORTED honestly, never the investment result itself.
summary.action: When reading an investment pitch, always ask: is this figure a full composite, or just the best fund picked out to be shown off?

application.title: A second look at investment advertising
application.message: Next time you see an advertised "X% a year" from a fund manager, look for whether the figure is stated as the performance of the WHOLE portfolio or composite, or of one specific fund or account that was chosen.
application.secondary: Vagueness about where a performance figure came from is a warning sign that calls for caution.

sections.text: Have you ever seen an advertisement for "fund X, returning 40% a year" and wondered whether the number could be trusted? GIPS Standards are the framework built to answer that question systematically.
What GIPS is and why it exists

The Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) are a voluntary set of standards built by CFA Institute that govern how investment management firms must calculate and present their investment performance. Before GIPS existed, each firm could pick whatever calculation method flattered it most - which left firms impossible to compare fairly and, worse, created room to dress up the numbers to attract investors.
The composite: the heart of GIPS

The most important principle in GIPS is the concept of the "composite" - a fund manager must group ALL accounts and funds sharing the same investment objective and strategy into one composite, and then report the weighted-average performance of that entire composite. This blocks a common practice: picking out the best-performing fund from the dozens under management to put into marketing material, while staying silent about the weak ones.

sections.label: A concrete example
sections.text: A firm runs 20 growth equity funds. Without GIPS, it could advertise only the fund returning 45% a year (the best one) and never mention the other 19, which may have managed just 8-15% a year. Under GIPS, it must report the weighted-average performance of ALL 20 funds in the "growth equity" composite, which produces a far more honest figure.
GIPS is voluntary, but it cannot be done halfway

What makes GIPS unusual: no firm is compelled by law to follow it. But once a firm claims to be "GIPS-compliant", it must comply fully and consistently with every requirement of the framework - it cannot apply the convenient parts and skip the inconvenient ones. This is exactly why large institutional investors (pension funds, endowments, insurance funds) tend to treat GIPS compliance as the first screen when assessing a prospective fund manager.

items: GIPS is a voluntary standard rather than a law, but once a firm commits it must comply in full
The composite - grouping every account on a shared strategy - is the core tool against cherry-picked numbers
GIPS compliance is often a precondition before a large institutional investor will consider allocating capital
GIPS guarantees honesty in HOW PERFORMANCE IS REPORTED, not that the actual investment results will be good

lines: GIPS is not a tool for predicting future performance; it is a tool for making sure you are comparing apples with apples, not apples with carefully selected fruit.
Next time you read an impressive performance figure, ask yourself: is this a full GIPS composite, or just one handsome apple that was picked out?

The aim: fair comparison between fund managers

realWorldExample.description: Many large asset managers around the world state publicly that their performance reporting "complies with GIPS" as a way of building credibility with institutional investors - because large institutions (pension funds, endowments) commonly demand evidence of GIPS compliance as a precondition before they will even consider handing over capital, precisely because GIPS removes the risk of dressed-up figures.

quiz.question: Are the GIPS Standards a law that every fund manager must follow?
options: Mandatory only in the US, and entirely unnecessary anywhere else
Yes, every investment management firm is required to comply
No - GIPS is voluntary, but once claimed it must be met in full
Mandatory only for funds above one trillion dong in size
quiz.explanation: GIPS is a voluntary standard - no firm is compelled by law to follow it. But here is the important part: once a firm has claimed to be "GIPS-compliant", it must comply fully and consistently, and cannot apply the parts that suit it. The two "mandatory only" options invent a threshold the framework does not contain: GIPS has no geographic carve-out and no size test, so a small firm and a giant one face identical requirements once either claims compliance. The blanket "yes" fails for the same reason from the opposite direction - it mistakes a professional standard for legislation.

quiz.question: What is the concept of a "composite" in GIPS for?
options: Composite is the term for how a fund's management fee is calculated
Composite applies only to bond funds, never to equity funds
Composite is the name of a large aggregate stock market index
Grouping all accounts sharing one strategy into a single report
quiz.explanation: The composite is the core reporting unit of GIPS: group every account with the same investment strategy ("large-cap growth equity", for instance) into one composite, then report the weighted-average performance of that WHOLE composite - which removes the opportunity to select the attractive number. The fee-calculation answer confuses a reporting unit with a pricing mechanism. The bond-only answer invents an asset-class limit that would defeat the purpose, since equity strategies are where selection bias bites hardest. And the index answer borrows the word from a different context entirely - a composite here is built by the firm out of its own accounts, not by an exchange.

quiz.question: Why do large pension funds and endowments usually demand evidence of GIPS compliance before allocating capital to a manager?
options: Because GIPS makes performance consistent and comparable across firms
Because GIPS guarantees that a compliant fund will out-earn the market
Because it is a binding legal requirement imposed in every country worldwide
Because it is an arbitrary requirement with no specific reason at all
quiz.explanation: GIPS does not guarantee good performance; it guarantees that reported performance figures are HONEST and COMPARABLE. That is why large institutional investors, who have to compare dozens of managers against one another, treat GIPS compliance as an important first screen. The "guarantees outperformance" answer is the single most common misreading of the standard - it confuses how a number is produced with how large the number turns out to be. The legal-requirement answer is wrong because GIPS is voluntary everywhere, and the "arbitrary" answer ignores that the screen exists precisely to make a comparison possible at all.

quiz.question: A GIPS-compliant firm wants to market the record of its growth equity strategy. How must it present it?
options: The performance of accounts most representative of the strategy
The whole composite's performance, including the weaker accounts
The performance of the longest-running account in the strategy
The average across accounts still open at the publication date
quiz.explanation: The composite must contain every portfolio following the same strategy, including accounts that have been closed - that is exactly what stops cherry-picking. Choosing only the accounts a firm calls "representative" reintroduces the selection the composite was built to remove, since the firm decides what counts as representative. Choosing the longest-running account substitutes survivorship for strategy. And averaging only accounts still open at the publication date is survivorship bias in its purest form: the accounts that performed worst are also the ones most likely to have been closed, so excluding them lifts the figure without a single false number being written.

quiz.question: GIPS requires performance to be presented net of which fees?
options: After every fee, tax and cost that an individual investor bears
Before any fees at all, so investors apply their own fee schedule
After trading costs, stating whether it is gross or net of fees
After management fees, with trading costs presented separately
quiz.explanation: The standard requires trading costs to be deducted and requires an explicit statement of whether the figure is gross or net of fees, so the reader knows what is being compared. The core of GIPS is not that numbers must look good but that they must be comparable across firms. Deducting taxes and every investor-specific cost is impossible to standardise, because tax position differs by investor. Presenting everything before fees removes the one deduction the standard treats as non-negotiable. And leaving trading costs to be shown "at will" hands the firm back the discretion that made comparison impossible in the first place.

keyTakeaways: GIPS is a voluntary CFA Institute standard, but once compliance is claimed it must be complete, never selective
The "composite" concept - pooling every account on the same strategy - is the core tool against showing off only the best fund
Large institutional investors commonly treat GIPS compliance as a precondition for comparing managers fairly

practicePrompt.question: Which of the following matches the content of this lesson?
options: GIPS is a law that every fund manager in the world is required to follow
A composite groups every account on one strategy for honest reporting
GIPS guarantees that any compliant fund will deliver good performance
GIPS applies only to funds that are publicly listed on a stock exchange
practicePrompt.explanation: A composite pools every account following the same investment strategy so that an honest average performance can be reported, which prevents only the best fund being selected for advertising. The other three each fail on a point the lesson makes directly: GIPS is voluntary rather than legislated, it constrains how performance is calculated and disclosed rather than what the performance turns out to be, and it covers a firm's discretionary accounts generally rather than only listed vehicles.
